study_identification_part.si4_title: Using normative modeling and machine learning for detecting mild traumatic brain injury from magnetoencephalography data

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Support vector machine (SVM) with radial basis function (RBF) kernel for classification of mTBI patients vs controls; nested cross-validation (5-fold inner loop for hyperparameter tuning, 7-fold outer loop for evaluation, repeated 5 times for total of 35 folds); hyperparameters C (1, 5, 10) and γ (0.1, 0.01, 0.001) tested; class weighting inversely proportional to frequencies; data centered by median and scaled to IQR; hierarchical clustering with Spearman correlations to reduce feature multicollinearity; permutation feature importance to estimate feature significance; permutation tests (1000 iterations) for statistical significance (p < 0.05); Mann-Whitney U-test to assess differences in decision function scores between patients with/without visible MRI lesions; comparison of correctly vs incorrectly classified subjects; correlation with patient demographics (timing of MEG recording, RPQ score).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The SVM classifier achieved 79.0% accuracy in distinguishing mTBI patients from healthy controls using deviation scores from normative MEG power spectra, with theta-band (4-8 Hz) features in parietal, temporal, and occipital regions providing the most significant discriminative features.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using normative modeling combined with SVM classification, the study achieved 79.0% accuracy (sensitivity 91.2%, specificity 63.8%) in distinguishing 25 mTBI patients from 20 healthy controls. The best performance was obtained using the full normative dataset (N=621) across all ages, outperforming age-matched (76.1% accuracy) and random subset (71.1% accuracy) approaches. Classification without normative data yielded comparable accuracy (78.6%). Theta-band (4-8 Hz) activity provided the most significant features for classification, consistent with previous literature associating low-frequency activity with axonal injury. The most important discriminative features were located in parietal regions (supramarginal gyrus, postcentral gyrus, superior and inferior parietal lobule, precuneus), with additional contributions from temporal and occipital lobes. Eight patients showed aberrant theta activity exceeding 2 SD from the normative mean, and these were classified with 95.0% accuracy. Only two patients were consistently misclassified, both measured relatively late post-injury (3.5-4 months) with below-average RPQ scores. Three of 20 controls showed increased theta activity and were incorrectly classified as patients. No significant difference in decision function output was found between patients with and without visible MRI lesions (p=0.52, Mann-Whitney U-test). The results demonstrate the feasibility of using normative modeling of MEG data for individual-level diagnosis of mTBI, with interpretable deviation maps that could aid clinical decision-making.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Small clinical dataset (N=45 total); large standard deviations in performance metrics (0.15-0.32) limiting robustness; simple Z-score approach rather than sophisticated methods like Gaussian process regression; site differences between normative and clinical data not harmonized; manual ICA component inspection required (not fully automated); heterogeneity in injury location, timing, and symptoms; some patients likely recovered to normal function making 100% accuracy unrealistic; deviation values for controls slightly below zero due to site differences; limited specificity as low-frequency abnormalities can occur from causes other than mTBI.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Large functional imaging datasets from clinical populations are, however, rarely available, and drawing reliable conclusions about classification results is often hindered by the small size of the datasets. In this study, the effect of the dataset size was most clearly seen in the large standard deviations of the accuracy, sensitivity and specificity scores, which ranged from 0.15 to 0.32. ... The deviation values for the control subjects are overall slightly lower compared to the normative dataset, which might be an effect of different measurement sites. ... One limiting factor in translating research on candidate biomarkers for detecting mTBI from MEG data to clinical settings are the sometimes complex analysis pipelines, which may be time-consuming or require extensive expertise. Here, the analysis was automated with the exception of artefact removal, which required manual inspection of the ICA components ... such deviations from the normal range can occur also from other causes (ie. the deviations are not specific to mTBI).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Data segmentation using sliding window (200s length, 50s stride) resulting in 7 time series per subject for robustness; cross-validation splits constructed to avoid data leakage (samples from same subject only in training or validation, never both); predicted class label determined by majority vote across segments; comparison of full normative data vs age-matched vs random subset to explore optimal reference cohort selection; comparison to classification without normative data to assess added value; visual comparison of individual Z-score maps to findings from earlier study (Kaltiainen et al.) for reliability assessment; feature selection via hierarchical clustering to reduce multicollinearity before permutation importance calculation; cortical visualization of feature importance for interpretability.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a MEG-based normative modeling study, different from the typical MRI-based studies in this systematic review. The normative modeling served as a feature engineering step for supervised machine learning rather than being the primary diagnostic tool. The study used a publicly available normative dataset (Cam-CAN) which could facilitate reproducibility. The clinical measurements were performed 1-26 weeks post-injury (median ~8 weeks), with 19/25 within 9 weeks (subacute stage). Nine patients had follow-up at 6 months but these data were not analyzed due to small sample size. 60% (15/25) of patients had visible lesions in MRI. GCS scores ranged 14-15 (mean 14.4). RPQ scores ranged 3-36 (mean 17.2). The code to reproduce findings is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8360527. MEG data from mTBI patients and controls are not publicly available due to privacy concerns but can be shared with collaborators via ethics committee approval and data transfer agreement (contact: eettinen.toimikunta@hus.fi).
